The main reason is climate change. Unusually warm water makes corals push out the algae that live in their tissue and feed them. The coral turns white ("bleaches"), and if the heat lasts too long, it dies. In 2024 the reef had its worst heat stress on record, which caused the most widespread and severe bleaching ever seen there [1][2]. The next year's surveys found the biggest one-year drop in coral cover since records began, with regional losses of 14–30% and some reefs losing up to about 71% [2][3]. Cyclones, flooding and outbreaks of the coral-eating crown-of-thorns starfish add to the damage. The worst-hit corals are fast-growing Acropora, because they're sensitive to heat and are the starfish's favourite food [2][3].

Calling the reef "dying" goes a bit too far, though. It's badly stressed and swinging more wildly than before, but it isn't dead. The 2025/26 surveys found coral cover holding steady or rising slightly in the north and centre, falling slightly in the south, and at around 26–35% overall. That's the start of recovery from the 2024 bleaching, helped by a late-summer monsoon that cooled the water [4]. The worry is that bleaching, floods, cyclones and starfish are hitting more often and on top of each other. That leaves corals less and less time to recover between hits [4].
